questions.q: Roughly what share of BC's land is held by the provincial Crown?
choices: About 5%
About 50%
About 94%
About 99%
questions.explain: About 94% is provincial Crown land, about 1% is federal Crown land, and only about 5% is privately owned.
questions.ref: Lesson 3 · Who owns the land in BC?

questions.q: What changed on 21 May 2024 for First Nations land holding in BC?
choices: All reserves were transferred into the Land Title Act system
Recognized First Nations can register land in their own name
Treaty negotiations in BC formally ended for all First Nations
Aboriginal title became saleable to private buyers
questions.explain: Amendments to the Land Title Act and Property Law Act let First Nations such as Indian Act bands acquire and register fee simple and other interests directly, without corporations or trustees.
questions.ref: Lesson 3 · Who owns the land in BC?

questions.q: To prove Aboriginal title, what must a First Nation show?
choices: Present-day occupation only, with no historical evidence needed
Regular, exclusive use before Crown sovereignty (plus continuity)
A registered Crown grant issued to the Nation's ancestors
Payment of property taxes on the land for at least 20 years
questions.explain: Tsilhqot'in (2014) requires regular and exclusive pre-sovereignty use. If present use is relied on as evidence, continuity with pre-sovereignty occupation must also be shown.
questions.ref: Lesson 3 · Who owns the land in BC?

questions.q: What was significant about the 2025 Haida Title Lands Agreement?
choices: It was the first court declaration of Aboriginal title in Canada
It was the first federal recognition of title by negotiation
It created the first modern treaty signed in British Columbia
It moved Haida Gwaii into the federal Indian Land Registry
questions.explain: The agreement recognized Haida Aboriginal title on Haida Gwaii, the first time Canada did so by negotiation rather than a court order.
questions.ref: Lesson 3 · Who owns the land in BC?

questions.q: A homeowner wants to sell the back 3 metres of their lot to a neighbour. Which is true?
choices: It's not a subdivision because no new homes are being built
It's a subdivision and must comply with the Land Title Act
Owners have a common law right to do this without approval
Only a strata corporation can approve it
questions.explain: Any division of land into parcels is a subdivision. LTA s.73 extinguished the common law right to subdivide, so it must comply with the Act and get approval.

questions.q: A developer markets units as "townhouses" and has filed a strata plan. Legally, what are they?
choices: Townhouses, a separate legal category
Strata lots, because a strata plan was filed
Fee simple lots in a traditional subdivision
Leasehold interests only
questions.explain: "Townhouse" has no legal meaning. If a strata plan is filed, strata lots and common property are created, whatever the buildings look like.

questions.q: In a building strata development, what happens to the land under the building?
choices: It's owned by the developer forever
It becomes common property
It's divided among the strata lots by area
It goes to the municipality
questions.explain: In a building strata, the lots are carved out of the building, and the land becomes part of the common property.

questions.q: In a bare land strata development, the internal road needs repaving. Who pays?
choices: The municipality, because roads are public infrastructure
The strata lot owners, because the road is common property
The original developer, for as long as any lots are unsold
The province, through the Ministry of Transportation
questions.explain: Unlike a traditional subdivision where roads belong to the municipality, a bare land strata's road is usually common property, so the owners pay for it.

questions.q: When considering a strata conversion of an existing rental building, which is NOT something the approving council must consider?
choices: Priority of rental housing in the area
Proposals for relocating current occupants
The building's life expectancy
The developer's expected profit margin
questions.explain: The approving authority must consider rental housing priority, relocation of occupants and the building's life expectancy, among other things. Profit isn't one of the listed considerations.

questions.q: Two owners of a duplex strata can't agree on repairs. Which statement is correct?
choices: The Strata Property Act doesn't apply to two-unit properties
Same legal rules as a large strata; disputes can go to the CRT
A government strata inspector will step in and decide
Only the BC Supreme Court can hear disputes in a duplex strata
questions.explain: "A strata is a strata": the same legislation applies to a duplex (Whiting v. Peters). Stratas are self-enforcing, and the CRT is usually the preferred forum.

questions.q: Does the Strata Property Act apply to developments on Indian Act reserve land?
choices: Yes, the Act applies to all land in BC, including reserves
No; reserves are federal, so projects usually use long leases
Only for commercial projects on reserve land
Only if the First Nation has adopted its own land code
questions.explain: Provincial strata legislation doesn't apply on reserves, except through designated leasehold landlords such as the Sechelt Indian Band. It does apply on treaty lands, which are no longer reserves.

questions.q: When must a Schedule of Voting Rights be filed with a strata plan?
choices: Always, with every strata plan that's deposited
Only if a strata lot is non-residential
Only for bare land strata plans with no buildings
Only for leasehold strata plans on Crown land
questions.explain: The Schedule of Unit Entitlement is always filed; a Schedule of Voting Rights is needed only if at least one strata lot is non-residential.

questions.q: In a leasehold strata, what is the minimum term of the ground lease?
choices: 25 years
50 years
99 years
There is no minimum
questions.explain: Leasehold stratas can only be created on land leased for at least 50 years, from leasehold landlords such as governments, certain First Nations and universities.

questions.q: Under Strata Property Act s.68, where is the boundary of a strata lot in a building?
choices: The inside face of the walls, floors and ceilings
The outside face of the walls, floors and ceilings
The centre of the walls, floors and ceilings
Wherever the strata corporation's bylaws say
questions.explain: In a building strata, the boundary is the midpoint of each wall, floor or ceiling separating the lot from another lot, the common property or another parcel.

questions.q: What does nemo dat quod non habet mean?
choices: Let the former decision stand
No one can give what they don't have
It is not my deed
Let the buyer beware
questions.explain: Nemo dat: you can't transfer a better title than you hold. At common law, a forged deed broke the chain of title for everyone after it.

questions.q: Why didn't deeds recording systems solve the void deed problem?
choices: They weren't open to the public, so buyers couldn't search them
Recording a deed didn't make it valid; forgeries stayed void
They only recorded mortgages, not transfers of ownership
They were abolished in 1858 before they could be tested
questions.explain: Recording kept documents safe but didn't change their legal effect. A void deed stayed void, so innocent buyers still bore the risk.

questions.q: Marta forges a transfer of Anton's property to herself, then gives it as a gift to Clara, who knows nothing. Who's entitled to the property?
choices: Clara, because she's now the registered owner
Anton, because a gift isn't valuable consideration
Marta, because she was registered before the gift
The Crown, because the title is void
questions.explain: LTA s.25.1 protects a transferee under a void instrument only if they acted in good faith and gave valuable consideration. A gift (or $1) doesn't qualify.

questions.q: Marta (a forger) sells Anton's property at market value to Clara, who's honest and registers. What's the outcome?
choices: Anton recovers the property because a forged transfer is void
Clara keeps it; Anton may claim from the assurance fund
The sale is void and Clara's purchase money is returned
Clara and Anton become tenants in common of the property
questions.explain: A good-faith purchaser for valuable consideration who registers gets an indefeasible fee simple. Anton's remedy is the assurance fund, if he can't recover from Marta.

questions.q: Which of these binds a buyer even though it does NOT appear on title?
choices: An unregistered 5-year lease held by a tenant in occupation
A mineral reservation in the original Crown grant
An unregistered private easement used by a neighbour
An unregistered second mortgage owed to a private lender
questions.explain: Reservations in the original Crown grant are an exception to indefeasibility (LTA s.23). An unregistered lease binds only if it's 3 years or less with actual occupation.

questions.q: Which is NOT one of the exceptions to indefeasibility in LTA s.23?
choices: Unpaid municipal charges
A lease of 3 years or less with actual occupation
Fraud by the registered owner
An unregistered agreement to sell signed 10 years ago
questions.explain: Taxes and municipal charges, short occupied leases and fraud by the registered owner are all s.23 exceptions. An old unregistered agreement is not.

questions.q: What did the BC Court of Appeal decide in Gill v. Bucholtz (2009)?
choices: Registered mortgages are indefeasible, just like fee simple titles
Charges aren't indefeasible; the fraudster's mortgages were discharged
The assurance fund must compensate every innocent lender
Title insurance became mandatory for all BC purchases
questions.explain: Indefeasibility in BC protects the fee simple, not charges. The rightful owner got clear title back, and the court said lenders, not the public, should bear the cost of fraud.

questions.q: Alan gives Royal Bank a mortgage on December 1 (not registered) and CIBC a mortgage on December 4 (registered). Who has priority?
choices: Royal Bank, because its mortgage is older
CIBC, because it registered
They share priority equally
Neither, because both are void
questions.explain: Under LTA s.20, an unregistered instrument doesn't pass an interest against third parties. CIBC's registered mortgage takes priority, though Royal Bank can still sue Alan.

questions.q: Under LTA s.29, when is a buyer who knew about an unregistered interest NOT protected?
choices: Whenever they knew about the interest at any time before closing
When knowledge is combined with dishonest conduct amounting to fraud
Never; s.29 protects every registered buyer without exception
Only if the unregistered interest was a mortgage or other charge
questions.explain: Knowledge alone isn't fraud. Courts look for knowledge plus dishonest conduct, judged at the time the contract is formed (e.g. Woodwest Developments).

questions.q: Which is a requirement for a claim against the assurance fund?
choices: The claimant must have bought title insurance at closing
The claimant can't recover the loss by suing someone else
The claimant must be a lender rather than an owner
The loss must exceed $100,000 to qualify for a claim
questions.explain: The fund is a last resort. The claimant must show they lost an interest due to another's registration, would have recovered it at common law, and can't recover by other court action.

questions.q: A registered survey plan turns out to show the wrong lot dimensions, and the owner loses part of the expected land. Can they claim from the assurance fund?
choices: Yes, the assurance fund guarantees all registered plans
No, the land title office doesn't guarantee plan accuracy
Only if the error in the plan is greater than 10%
Only for strata plans, not for subdivision plans
questions.explain: The accuracy of registered plans (boundaries and dimensions) isn't guaranteed, so no claim can be made against the fund for those errors.

questions.q: What is a PID?
choices: The number assigned to a strata plan when deposited
A permanent 9-digit parcel identifier for a title
The property's BC Assessment roll number
The file number given to a builders lien
questions.explain: The PID is a 9-digit number that stays with the parcel unless it's subdivided or consolidated. It's the best way to search title, and it appears on the property tax notice.

questions.q: The standard BC contract of purchase and sale promises title free and clear EXCEPT for which of these?
choices: Any private easement registered in favour of a neighbour
A registered builders lien from unpaid renovation work
Covenants and rights of way for utilities or public bodies
A registered judgment obtained against the seller
questions.explain: The standard Title clause excepts Crown grant reservations, covenants and rights of way for utilities and public authorities, and listed tenancies. Other charges must be cleared or expressly approved by the buyer.

questions.q: A licensee attached a seller-supplied title search that was missing a page with seven charges restricting building. What happened in the 2016 discipline case?
choices: No penalty, because the conveyancer was responsible for title
A 14-day suspension, a course and $1,500 in costs
Licence cancelled permanently for misrepresentation
A written warning only, kept on the licensee's file
questions.explain: She breached the duties to discover relevant facts and to act with reasonable care. The lesson: get the complete title search yourself.

questions.q: The title shows a duplicate certificate of title is outstanding. What's the risk?
choices: None; a duplicate is just a souvenir copy of the title
The registrar won't register a transfer until it's returned
The property can't be insured until the duplicate is found
The seller's mortgage is automatically discharged on sale
questions.explain: With a duplicate out, transfers, mortgages and long-term leases won't be registered until it's returned. Locate it before the contract is written; replacing a lost one is slow.

questions.q: How long does a caveat stay on title before lapsing, unless the caveator starts a lawsuit and registers a CPL?
choices: 21 days
2 months
1 year
2 years
questions.explain: A caveat lapses automatically after two months. To keep the claim alive, the caveator must sue and register a certificate of pending litigation within that time.

questions.q: An owner paid the general contractor in full, but an unpaid electrical subcontractor files a builders lien. Which is true?
choices: The lien is invalid because the owner never hired the subcontractor
Subcontractors have lien rights, so it affects the owner's title
Only general contractors can file liens under the Builders Lien Act
The lien automatically expires when the property is sold
questions.explain: Contractors, subcontractors and workers all have lien rights. Liens can even be filed after the property is sold, if within the filing deadline.

questions.q: An owner serves a Form 6 Notice to Commence Action on a lien claimant. How long does the claimant have to sue and register a CPL?
choices: 7 days
21 days
45 days
1 year
questions.explain: A registered lien normally lasts one year. A Form 6 notice shortens that: the claimant must sue and file a CPL within 21 days or the lien is discharged.

questions.q: How is a section 219 covenant different from a common law restrictive covenant?
choices: It can only be held by a neighbouring landowner
It can be positive or negative, held by a government
It doesn't need to be registered to bind later owners
It expires automatically after 2 years unless renewed
questions.explain: LTA s.219 covenants are registered in favour of government bodies and, unlike common law restrictive covenants, can impose positive obligations.

questions.q: What does a Community Charter s.57 notice on title indicate?
choices: The property is a designated heritage site
The property may be unsafe due to bylaw or code breaches
A strata conversion has been approved by council
A water licence on the property has been cancelled
questions.explain: A s.57 notice appears under Legal Notations as a last resort when a property doesn't comply with bylaws or building rules (failed inspections, unpermitted work, former grow-ops). Contact the municipality.

questions.q: On completion, when does the deposit in the brokerage's trust account become the seller's money and the commission become earned?
choices: When the contract of purchase and sale is signed by both parties
When all of the buyer's subject conditions have been removed
When the transfer documents are submitted for registration
When the new title is issued, usually 7 to 14 days later
questions.explain: Once the transfer is submitted for registration, the seller has no further claim to title and the buyer none to the deposit. Commission is earned at that point.

questions.q: A lender requires title insurance on a purchase. Who does that policy protect?
choices: The owner and the lender equally, up to the purchase price
The lender only; the owner needs a separate owner's policy
The owner only, since the owner paid the premium
The real estate brokerage, against negligence claims
questions.explain: A lender's policy protects the lender. An owner who wants coverage must pay for an owner's policy.

questions.q: Which is the safest way to verify a change in a client's payment instructions received by email?
choices: Reply to the email asking the client to confirm
Call the phone number given in the new email
Call the client on a number you already had
Go ahead if the email includes the client's full name
questions.explain: Email and text accounts can be hacked. Verify in person or by phone using a trusted number, never one supplied in the instruction itself.

questions.q: Which combination is a classic title fraud red flag?
choices: A local seller who wants a full MLS® listing with a sign
An overseas owner wanting a quick, quiet, cheap sale by POA
A seller who shows original photo ID in person at the office
A seller with a long, well-documented mortgage history
questions.explain: Changed contact methods, urgency, unusual listing requests, new or scanned ID and powers of attorney are all key red flags.

questions.q: Which is true of the Ministry of Environment's Site Registry?
choices: It's part of the land title system and appears on every title
It's separate from title and especially important for commercial
It's free and searched automatically with every title search
It lists all designated heritage sites in the province
questions.explain: The Site Registry records contaminated site information under the Environmental Management Act. It's entirely separate from title and is key due diligence for commercial deals.

questions.q: How does the manufactured home registry differ from the Torrens land title system?
choices: It has indefeasibility like Torrens, but no assurance fund
It just records ownership: no title or assurance fund
It's identical to the land title system in every respect
It only records security interests, never ownership
questions.explain: The Manufactured Home Act registry is a registration system, not Torrens. It records ownership but doesn't guarantee it.

questions.q: Before offering a used manufactured home for sale, which sticker must you confirm is present?
choices: The MHR registration sticker only, with nothing else needed
A valid CSA (or equivalent) electrical label, or a silver label
A municipal business licence sticker for the park
A home inspector's sticker from the last inspection
questions.explain: BCFSA warns that a manufactured home can't be offered for sale without a valid electrical certification label. The MHR sticker is only an ID number, like a VIN.

questions.q: A seller asks the park landlord for consent to assign their pad tenancy to the buyer. The landlord doesn't reply within 10 days. What's the result?
choices: Consent is deemed to be refused
Consent is deemed to be given
The buyer must move the home off the pad
The pad tenancy ends automatically
questions.explain: Under the Manufactured Home Park Tenancy Regulation, the landlord must respond in writing within 10 days (unless extended by agreement), or is deemed to consent.
